summary:
Katsina State stands under the national framework of Nigeria: the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014 (SSMPA) applies nationwide and reaches beyond marriage, banning cohabitation between same-sex partners, any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship and the operation of gay organisations, with 10 to 14 years' imprisonment. Human Rights Watch (October 2016) records that police have used the Act to justify torture and arbitrary arrest. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on Nigeria (version 4.0, June 2025) records same-sex sex between men as criminalised under secular law with up to 14 years' imprisonment, and a Sharia criminal layer applying in twelve northern states whose provisions extend to women.

Katsina operates that religious layer through its own statute: the Sharia Penal Code Law 2001, Law No. 2 of 2001, coming into operation on 20 June 2001 and gazetted in Katsina State Gazette Vol. 12 No. 23 of 27 August 2001. Ostien's annotated volume records Katsina among the three states, with Kaduna and Kebbi, whose sodomy text reads: whoever commits the offence of sodomy shall be punished with stoning to death (rajm).

Sexual acts between women carry a death maximum here as well. A footnote in the same annotated volume shows that only Kano and Katsina reach stoning to death as the maximum punishment for the lesbianism offence, against the harmonised northern code's base of 50 lashes and up to six months' imprisonment. Katsina is therefore one of only two states whose law carries death as the maximum for same-sex acts between women as well as between men.

Trans identity itself is not explicitly criminalised in the national statute, but gender expression is exposed. Reuters (September 2022) reports that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public, and the sources available here do not settle whether those proposals have been enacted. The cross-dressing layer that is documented applies to men who dress or behave as women, who face prison or a fine; a Kano court sentenced a TikToker to one year in prison over a cross-dressing video on 20 June 2025. In the Sharia-governed northern states generally, punishments for same-sex conduct range from lashing or caning to capital punishment.

Violence against perceived trans people has gone unpunished. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, a TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on a highway in Abuja hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing. The Dial (February 2025) records that six months after the killing no suspects had been charged.

Police violence against people read as gay or trans is routine. TimesLIVE (March 2025) reports that Okafor, a 24-year-old stopped by Lagos police, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay. Visitors who use dating apps face a parallel risk: the Thomson Reuters Foundation (April 2024) documents kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and similar apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people, and the UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's 2026 travel advice, as reported by Sahara Reporters, warns LGBT+ travellers of attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty risk under Sharia law in northern states.

The clearest documented case of a trans prisoner's placement concerns Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), Nigeria's most prominent transgender woman. She pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024 and was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, served in a maximum-security prison in Lagos before release on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly asked which prison the authorities would keep the crossdresser in, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to discretion. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.
tangentialFactors:
Human Rights Watch (2004) traces the spread of Sharia adoption across northern Nigeria from Zamfara's Shari'a Establishment Law, promulgated on 27 October 1999 and in force from 27 January 2000, and lists twelve states concerned: Bauchi, Borno, Gombe, Jigawa, Kaduna, Kano, Katsina, Kebbi, Niger, Sokoto, Yobe and Zamfara. The provisions cited in that report remain in force.

The UK Home Office note describes Nigeria as operating a hybrid legal system, with a secular criminal code alongside a Sharia criminal layer in twelve northern states. Nigeria's LGBTQ+ framework carries no protective legislation of any kind, and the SSMPA reinforced criminalisation inherited from the colonial period rather than replacing it.

The cross-dressing conviction recorded in Kano on 20 June 2025 shows how the gender-expression offence is being used in practice across the northern states. Only two of the twelve, Kano and Katsina, carry a death maximum for the offence concerning women, which places Katsina at the severe end of the northern penalty structure rather than in its middle.
localsOnly:
Residents of Katsina State face two overlapping criminal regimes: the national SSMPA and the state's Sharia Penal Code Law 2001, which is a Katsina statute gazetted in Katsina State Gazette Vol. 12 No. 23 of 27 August 2001 and in operation since 20 June 2001. The stoning-to-death maximum for sodomy and the death maximum for the lesbianism offence apply to persons within the state, not only to visitors.

Placement of a trans or gender-nonconforming detainee between male and female sections in Katsina is not governed by any published housing rule, segregation policy or women's-wing measure in the sources reviewed. In the one documented Nigerian precedent, placement was left to prison discretion and later found unlawful for unrelated reasons by an October 2024 investigative panel under the Nigerian Correctional Service Act.

Arrest data for these offences is limited, so the frequency of enforcement in Katsina cannot be established from these sources; the penalty structure and its severity are documented, while day-to-day enforcement practice is not.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether the proposals to criminalise public cross-dressing reported by Reuters in September 2022 have been enacted nationally remains unresolved in the sources available here. The Kato cross-dressing conviction of 20 June 2025 is recorded for Kano, not Katsina; no Katsina cross-dressing prosecution is sourced.

The Wikipedia overview article on LGBTQ+ people in prison contains no Nigeria or Katsina entry at all: a full-text scan returns zero mentions, and its discussion of placement-by-gender-identity norms elsewhere does not extend to this jurisdiction. No Katsina-specific trans-prisoner housing policy, special unit or segregation-for-placement practice is documented in any source reviewed, and the absence in Wikipedia is negative evidence only, not confirmation that no such practice exists.

Arrest and prosecution counts for same-sex offences in Katsina are not available: the UK Home Office note states that arrest data for these offences is limited. It is also unresolved which section of a Katsina correctional facility a person placed as female would be held in.
